Title: Speeding Up the Buildroot Build Process | Nayab Sayed
# Speeding Up the Buildroot Build Process. Speeding Up the Buildroot Build Process. I frequently need to build a fresh Buildroot target image, and it can be quite time-consuming, particularly when dealing with toolchain-related changes that necessitate starting from scratch. According to Buildroot’s documentation, there are few ways to expedite the build process for the Buildroot system. The typical steps for building an embedded Linux image for the Raspberry Pi 4 using Buildroot are as follows:. To do this, run *make menuconfig*, search for the string *BR2\_PER\_PACKAGE\_DIRECTORIES*, enable it, and save the configuration. Now, run *make clean && make -j`nproc`* to perform a top-level parallel build. You have the option to instruct Buildroot to use an external toolchain. The SDK/toolchain will be generated in the *output/images* directory. * Set *Toolchain URL* to the SDK downloaded path. * Set *External toolchain gcc version* -> Taken from above step. * Set *External toolchain kernel headers series* -> Taken from above step. * Set *External toolchain C library* -> Taken from above step (ex: glibc). After pointing Buildroot to the external toolchain, run the command *make clean && make -j`nproc`* .The build process took approximately *14m47s* to complete. For this testing purpose, intentionally I deleted download directory before running *make* command. To enable *ccache*, navigate to *make menuconfig* -> *Build options* -> *Enable compiler cache*. With ccache enabled, the build process stores object files created from source files in the default cache directory *$HOME/.buildroot-ccache*. In my case, when I initiated an incremental build using the commands *make clean* and *make -j`nproc`*, the entire build process only took 5 minutes and 24 seconds. Now also, the *dl* directory was deleted manually before building. In Buildroot, there’s a configuration option, *BR2\_DL\_DIR*, where you can set the value to use a shared downloads path for all target builds. Buildroot *Building out of tree* feature lets you construct images for multiple targets using the same Buildroot source tree. Now there are two output directories, named *rpi* and *mchp*, for each target, all utilizing the same Buildroot source tree. | BR2\_PER\_PACKAGE\_DIRECTORIES | make -j`nproc` | SDK | ccache | Downloads | Build Time |. | Enabled | Yes | External | Disabled | NA | 14m47s |.

results.content:
Title: Speeding up incremental changes with AWS SAM Accelerate and nested stacks | AWS Compute Blog
# Speeding up incremental changes with AWS SAM Accelerate and nested stacks. Developers and operators have been using the AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM) to author, build, test, and deploy serverless applications in AWS for over three years. As good as AWS SAM is at making your serverless development experience easier and faster, building non-trivial cloud applications remains a challenge. However, the latency of deploying an entire AWS CloudFormation stack for every code change is a challenge that developers face with this approach. In this blog post, I show how to increase development velocity by using AWS SAM Accelerate with AWS CloudFormation nested stacks. We recommend nested stacks for deploying complex serverless applications, which aligns to the Serverless Application Lens of the AWS Well-Architected Framework. AWS SAM Accelerate speeds up deployment from your local system by bypassing AWS CloudFormation to deploy code and resource updates when possible. ## AWS CloudFormation nested stacks and AWS SAM. With AWS SAM, developers create nested stacks using the AWS::Serverless::Application resource type. The following example shows a snippet from a template.yaml file, which is the root stack for an AWS SAM application. Each AWS::Serverless::Application resource type references a child stack, which is an independent AWS SAM template. However, when you synchronize code changes directly into the AWS Cloud, it can introduce drift between your CloudFormation stacks and its deployed resources. For this reason, you should only use AWS SAM Accelerate to publish changes in a development stack. After the deployment is complete, AWS SAM watches for local changes and synchronizes them to AWS. On save, AWS SAM notices the local code change, and updates the **CompleteOrder** Lambda function. In this example, AWS SAM Accelerate is 10–15 times faster than the CloudFormation deployment workflow (sam deploy) for single function code changes. The sam sync –watch command recognizes the configuration change requires a CloudFormation deployment to update the db nested stack. AWS SAM Accelerate helps builders achieve a high-fidelity development experience by rapidly synchronizing code changes into the AWS Cloud. This post shows AWS SAM Accelerate features that push code changes in near real time to a development environment in the Cloud.
